cultivar: Local Xiushui population bushes with Ningzhou-area selections and introduced Fujian cultivars
processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black, known for light withering, heavy rolling and full oxidation: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, then sieved, picked, re-fired and blended; the Jin Hao grade is made from early tippy pickings, and Long Xu Cha is hand-tied into bundles before drying.
harvest_season: Spring, starting before Qingming, with single buds and a bud with one leaf as the usual standard; early pickings make the tippy Jin Hao grade.
appearance_dry: Slim, tight, slightly curved dark strands with golden tips; Long Xu Cha comes as neat bundles tied with coloured silk thread.
appearance_liquor: Bright red with a golden rim.
appearance_wet: Even, tender copper-red leaves and buds.
taste_profile: Sweet and mellow with honey, light dried fruit and a clean, fresh finish; gentler and brighter than the heavier Hunan and Hubei blacks nearby.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at around 90 °C, short steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes. Long Xu Cha bundles go in a glass pot whole and are steeped repeatedly.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with Jin Hao as the top grade; drink within a year or two. Long Xu Cha bundles are a gift item made in small numbers each spring. Not aged.
description:
Ning Hong is the gongfu black of Xiushui in north-west Jiangxi, named after Fenning and Yining, the district's old names. It is one of the earliest of China's gongfu blacks: the craft is traced to the late Qianlong era and became famous in the early Daoguang years, which makes it decades older than Keemun, and from the mid nineteenth century it was a serious export tea. Like several inland blacks it later faded and is now a regional specialty rather than a household name.

It is made in the gongfu way, withering, rolling, oxidation, drying and sorting, with a house style of light withering, heavy rolling and full oxidation, and the top grade, Ning Hong Jin Hao, is picked early for golden tips. Its curiosity is Long Xu Cha, 'dragon whisker tea': a bundle of whole leaves tied at one end with coloured silk thread, dried as a tassel, and brewed whole in a glass pot so the leaves fan out.

In the cup it is sweet and mellow with honey and light dried fruit, a clean, slightly brisk finish and less weight than the Hunan and Hubei blacks across the border; it runs six or seven steeps at around 90 °C and makes a bright, easy pot. It is the kind of black tea that suits an afternoon rather than a breakfast.

It is sold as the current spring, mostly within Jiangxi and through a few specialists, with Jin Hao at the top and plainer numbered grades below. Look for slim, tight, tippy leaf and a sweet dry aroma; the Long Xu bundles are more about the show than the cup, but good ones are made from decent leaf and steep several times.

If you collect the old export names, Keemun, Congou, Ningchow, this is the tea behind the last of them.
sources_note: Origin dating (Daoguang era, early-to-mid 19th century) follows Chinese tea-history sources; cultivar information is generalised. 'Ningchow' is the historical trade spelling.
history:
Ning Hong comes from Xiushui in north-west Jiangxi, whose old names, Fenning and Yining, gave the tea its name. It counts among China's earlier gongfu blacks. The heritage record traces the craft to the late Qianlong era, says it became famous in the early Daoguang years and peaked under Guangxu, with exports from the mid nineteenth century. One Keemun origin story even has a founder hiring Ning Hong masters.

The craft joined the national intangible heritage list in 2021.
